import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 386
*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/386](https://www.erdosproblems.com/386)
-/


namespace Erdos386

open Nat

/--
There is a $k$, such that $2 \le k \le n - 2$ and
$\binom{n}{k}$ can be the product of consecutive primes infinitely often?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_386 :
    answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ k ≥ 2, ∃ᶠ n in .atTop,
      k ≤ n - 2 ∧ ∃ p q : ℕ, n.choose k = ∏ i ∈ .Ico p q, nth Nat.Prime i := by
    sorry

/--
For all $2 \le k \le n - 2$,
can $\binom{n}{k}$ be the product of consecutive primes infinitely often?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_386.variants.forall :
    answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ k ≥ 2, ∃ᶠ n in .atTop,
      k ≤ n - 2 ∧ ∃ p q : ℕ, n.choose k = ∏ i ∈ .Ico p q, nth Nat.Prime i := by
    sorry

/--
Can $\binom{n}{2}$ be the product of consecutive primes infinitely often?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_386.variants.two :
    answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ᶠ n in .atTop,
      2 ≤ n - 2 ∧ ∃ p q : ℕ, n.choose 2 = ∏ i ∈ .Ico p q, nth Nat.Prime i := by
    sorry

end Erdos386

findings.description: The quantifier order in lines 35–36 requires one fixed k ≥ 2 for which infinitely many n work: `∃ k ≥ 2, ∃ᶠ n in .atTop, ...`. The source asks whether there are infinitely many admissible binomial coefficients, allowing k to vary with n. An infinite solution family with unbounded min(k, n-k), but only finitely many solutions for each fixed k, is not covered by this Lean statement. Finiteness of the possible k in each individual row does not justify moving `∃ k` outside the infinitude quantifier. The main docstring introduces the same additional fixed-k restriction.
findings.source_evidence: https://www.erdosproblems.com/latex/386 states: “Let 2 ≤ k ≤ n−2. Can binom(n,k) be the product of consecutive primes infinitely often?” Erdős–Graham, Old and New Problems and Results in Combinatorial Number Theory (1980), p. 74, poses the general question and then separately discusses binom(n,2) (https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~ronspubs/80_11_number_theory.pdf). The source discussion also explicitly studies varying-k families, including the conclusion k=o(n): https://www.erdosproblems.com/forum/thread/386?order=oldest#post-151.
findings.suggested_fix: Move the existential quantifier for k inside `∃ᶠ n`: `answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ᶠ n : ℕ in Filter.atTop, ∃ k ≥ 2, k ≤ n - 2 ∧ ∃ p q : ℕ, n.choose k = ∏ i ∈ Finset.Ico p q, Nat.nth Nat.Prime i`. Update the main docstring accordingly. The existing statement can be retained as an explicitly named fixed-k variant.

reformulations.difference: The prime-product expression, shared by all three declarations, allows arbitrary endpoints p and q without explicitly requiring p < q.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Under 2 ≤ k and k ≤ n−2, Nat.choose_eq_one_iff implies n.choose k ≠ 1. If q ≤ p, Finset.Ico p q is empty and its product equals 1. Thus every actual witness already satisfies p < q. The scratch file proves the equivalence obtained by adding this condition. Separately, Nat.nth Nat.Prime is strictly increasing and enumerates every prime from 2, so these index intervals represent consecutive-prime blocks.

reformulations.difference: The explicit bound `2 ≤ n - 2` excludes n < 4 from the special infinitude question; the associated OEIS sequence includes the additional values 1 and 3.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Only finitely many n are excluded, which does not affect infinitude. The scratch file proves, for every fixed k and predicate P, `(∃ᶠ n in atTop, k ≤ n - 2 ∧ P n) ↔ (∃ᶠ n in atTop, P n)`. Applying this with k=2 verifies the equivalence.
